claims.text: Adding a controlled trace amount of an additional metallic element will enhance glass-forming ability in phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys.
Adding a controlled trace amount of an additional metallic element will enhance the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
The baseline alloy exhibits a metastable amorphous or partially crystalline state under typical cooling conditions.
The added element can interact preferentially with phosphorus.
The intervention is expected to be effective under rapid-quenching conditions used to produce metallic glasses.
The intervention is expected to improve behavior under annealing protocols used to assess thermal stability.
Preferential interactions between phosphorus and the added element induce local chemical ordering.
The trace addition promotes short-range ordering around phosphorus atoms.
Short-range ordering around phosphorus impedes crystallite nucleation during cooling.
The inhibited crystallite nucleation increases the crystallization temperature upon heating.
The modified alloy will have a lower critical cooling rate than the baseline alloy.
The modified alloy will have a higher crystallization onset temperature than the baseline alloy.
The improvement may disappear if the added-element concentration exceeds its solubility limit.
The hypothesis may fail if the added element does not interact selectively with phosphorus.
An adverse change in compositional balance or phase behavior may eliminate the proposed improvement.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as having an identical alloy composition while lacking the added element. Adding an element necessarily changes the composition unless the hypothesis specifies which constituent is reduced to compensate and defines 'identical' as referring only to the parent composition.
